title: Reformed also refuse creed-grade certainty and keep Calvin’s struggle with unbelief
source_text: XLVIII. Doctores vero Scholae Reformatae fatentur certitudinem quam habent fideles quod ipsorum fides & poenitentia vera & syncera sit, & ex consequenti quod sunt coram Deo justificati, non aequare certitudinem, quae requiritur in assensu quem articulis fidei debemus, & quo credere tenemur Christum esse Dei filium, & Mundi servatorem. Non negant etiam esse quendam timorem piae sollicitudinis securitati carnali oppositum, qui nunquam a fidelibus in hac vita abesse debet: imo saepe fideles de gratia Dei erga se dubitare atque formidare, neque hoc obstare tamen quominus fideles & justi maneant; adeoque non improbant Calvini verba quae leguntur in Antidoto Conc. Trid. ad Sess. 6. ubi loquens de eo quod experiuntur fideles in recognoscenda erga se gratia, Nec certe, inquit, dum fidem docemus esse debere certam & securam, eam certitudinem aliquam imaginamur, quae nulla tangitur dubitatione, nec securitatem, quae nulla inquietudine sollicitatur, quin potius dicimus perpetuum esse fidelibus certamen cum sua ipsorum infidelitate. Tantum abest, ut eorum conscientias in placida aliqua quiete collocemus, quae nullis omnino turbis interpellatur. Item, Sentit hanc in se divisionem suam pectus, quod partim ob divinae bonitatis agnitionem suavitate perfunditur: partim ob suae calamitatis sensum amaritudine angitur, & ob suae iniquitatis testimonium trepidat, & mortem exhorrescit; quae variatio ex fidei imperfectione contingit. Quae certe dum utrinque conceduntur atque proferuntur, in eo videntur partes dissidentes proxime ad se invicem accedere.
pass_a_gloss: But the doctors of the Reformed School confess that the certainty which the faithful have that their faith and repentance is true and sincere, and consequently that they are justified before God, does not equal the certainty which is required in the assent which we owe to the articles of faith, and by which we are bound to believe that Christ is the Son of God and Savior of the world. They also do not deny that there is a certain fear of pious solicitude opposed to carnal security, which ought never to be absent from the faithful in this life: nay, that the faithful often doubt and fear concerning God’s grace toward them, and that this nevertheless does not hinder them from remaining faithful and just; and so they do not disapprove Calvin’s words which are read in the Antidote to the Council of Trent at Sess. 6, where speaking of what the faithful experience in recognizing grace toward themselves he says: Nor certainly, while we teach that faith ought to be certain and secure, do we imagine some certainty which is touched by no doubt, nor a security which is solicited by no disquiet, but rather we say that there is a perpetual contest for the faithful with their own unbelief. So far are we from placing their consciences in some placid quiet which is interrupted by no troubles at all. Likewise, Its breast feels this division in itself, because partly on account of the recognition of divine goodness it is flooded with sweetness; partly on account of the sense of its calamity it is distressed with bitterness, and on account of the testimony of its iniquity it trembles, and shudders at death; which variation befalls from the imperfection of faith. Which things certainly, while they are conceded and brought forward on both sides, in this the dissenting parties seem to approach most nearly to one another.
pass_b_english: Reformed refuse to equate status-assurance with creed-assent and keep watchful fear.
Calvin’s Antidote—faith fights unbelief—lets Le Blanc draw the parties near.
